structure.title: A visitor hears a history
structure.text: Lockwood's arrival leads into Nelly Dean's account of the households and relationships that preceded him.

structure.title: Consequences across generations
structure.text: The narrative follows attachments, property, and injuries as they enter younger lives. Repeated names require attention to family position.

people.name: Heathcliff
people.text: A dark, ragged orphan found in the streets of Liverpool and brought home by old Mr Earnshaw, to the resentment of his son Hindley.

people.name: Catherine Earnshaw
people.text: Mr Earnshaw's wild, spirited daughter, who runs free on the moors with Heathcliff and is closer to him than to anyone.

people.name: Nelly Dean
people.text: The housekeeper who grew up at Wuthering Heights and tells its story to Lockwood, the new tenant, over the long winter evenings.

context.title: Stories through witnesses
context.text: The reader rarely receives an entirely unmediated event. Nelly and Lockwood have interests, limitations, and different distances from the people described.
context.takeaway: Ask who saw what is being reported.

context.title: Property and dependence
context.text: Houses and inheritance organise practical power. Passion acts through legal and domestic arrangements as well as declarations.
context.takeaway: Track who can remain in a home.

notice.why: An inherited pattern may be repeated or resisted.
The landscape makes belonging and exclusion physically felt.

opening: Heathcliff arrives at a Yorkshire farmhouse as a child nobody there knows what to do with. Catherine becomes his closest companion; her brother makes sure he understands his inferior place. The attachment growing between them absorbs the injuries around it, until love and the desire to hurt become dangerously entangled. Emily Brontë follows what happens when people refuse to let a grievance end with them, across houses, marriages, and children who inherit arrangements made long before they had any chance to object.
